### Key Takeaways

*   Private equity firms buy and overhaul companies to earn a profit or break them up and sell off parts.
*   Capital for acquisitions comes from outside investors in the private equity funds the firms establish and manage, usually supplemented by debt. Some or all of the debt is often placed on the balance sheet of the company being acquired.
*   The private equity industry has grown rapidly; it tends to be most popular when stock prices are high and interest rates are low.
*   Depending on the private equity firm’s skills and objectives, a private equity acquisition can make a company more competitive or saddle it with unsustainable debt.

Private equity describes investment partnerships that buy and manage companies before selling them. Private equity firms operate these investment funds on behalf of institutional and accredited investors.

Private equity funds may acquire private companies or public ones in their entirety, or invest in such buyouts as part of a consortium. They typically do not hold stakes in companies that remain listed on a stock exchange.

Private equity is often grouped with [venture capital](https://www.investopedia.com/terms/v/venturecapital.asp) and [hedge funds](https://www.investopedia.com/articles/02/111302.asp) as an alternative investment. Traditional private equity funds usually require significant capital commitments for years and are generally limited to institutions and qualifying investors, including many high-net-worth individuals. Some feeder and registered structures offer broader access.1

Mira Norian / Investopedia

## What Is Private Equity?

In contrast with venture capital, most private equity firms and funds invest in [mature companies](https://www.investopedia.com/terms/m/mature-firm.asp) rather than startups. They manage their portfolio companies to increase their worth or to extract value before exiting the investment years later. Private equity firms raise client capital to [launch private equity funds](https://www.investopedia.com/articles/markets/100515/how-start-your-own-private-equity-fund.asp) and operate them as [general partner](https://www.investopedia.com/ask/answers/062515/what-difference-between-silent-partner-and-general-partner.asp)s, managing fund investments in exchange for fees and a share of profits above a preset minimum known as the [hurdle rate](https://www.investopedia.com/terms/h/hurdlerate.asp).2 3

The private equity industry has had significant swings in recent years. In 2024, buyout investment value rebounded by 37% year over year to $602 billion, reflecting the industry’s resilience.4 The total announced global private equity deal volume increased 22% from $1.3 trillion in 2023 to $1.7 trillion in 2024, though volumes were still below pandemic-era levels.5

Image by Sabrina Jiang Â© Investopedia 2020

However, the industry is facing notable headwinds. Private equity assets under management fell by about 2% to $4.7 trillion in 2024—the first decline since tracking began in 2005, according to Bain & Co. This contraction highlights mounting challenges as investors confront an approximately $3.8 trillion backlog of aging and unsold deals. Global buyout distributions fell to an annualized 11% of net asset value based on data through the third quarter of 2024, the lowest level in more than a decade. Slowing distributions prompted limited partners to reduce new allocations.6 4

While funds typically start distributing profits after several years, recent data shows holding periods have lengthened significantly, with sponsors having the average holding period lengthening to five or more years from about 4.2 years earlier in the 2020s.7 8

Some high-profile investors have criticized the industry’s inability to exit investments and return capital, with continuation funds—where assets are sold from an existing fund to a new vehicle under the same sponsor rather than to an outside buyer—becoming a controversial practice. The [slowdown in exits](https://www.investopedia.com/the-industry-that-s-running-out-of-moves-11814247) has also affected fundraising, with global buyout funds raising 23% less in 2024 than in 2023. The decline continued by an additional 11% in 2025.9 4

### Fast Fact

To learn more about investing in private markets (and advising clients interested in doing so), see the rest of the series: [Private Market Edge](https://www.investopedia.com/how-to-talk-to-your-clients-about-private-market-investing-11791069).

## Private Equity Specialties

Some private equity firms and funds specialize in a particular category of private-equity deals. While venture capital is often listed as a subset of private equity, its distinct function and skillset set it apart, and have given rise to dedicated venture capital firms that dominate their sector. Other [private equity specialties](https://www.investopedia.com/articles/financial-careers/09/private-equity.asp) include:

*   [Distressed investing](https://www.investopedia.com/terms/d/distressedsecurities.asp), specializing in struggling companies with critical financing needs
*   Growth equity, funding expanding companies beyond their startup phase
*   Sector specialists, with some private equity firms focusing solely on technology or energy deals, for example
*   [Secondary buyouts](https://www.investopedia.com/terms/s/secondary-buyout.asp), involving the sale of a company owned by one private equity firm to another such firm
*   Carve-outs involving the purchase of corporate [subsidiaries](https://www.investopedia.com/terms/s/subsidiary.asp) or units.

## Private Equity Deal Types

The deals private equity firms make to buy and sell their portfolio companies can be divided into categories according to their circumstances.

The buyout remains a staple of private equity deals, involving the acquisition of a controlling stake in a company, whether public, [closely held](https://www.investopedia.com/terms/c/closely-held-corporation.asp), or privately owned. Private equity investors acquiring an underperforming public company will often seek to cut costs and may restructure its operations.

Another type of private equity acquisition is the carve-out, in which private equity investors buy a division of a larger company, typically a [noncore business](https://www.investopedia.com/terms/n/non-core-assets.asp) put up for sale by its parent corporation. Examples include Carlyle’s acquisition of Tyco Fire & Security Services Korea Co. Ltd. from Tyco International Ltd. in 2014, and Francisco Partners’ deal to acquire corporate training platform Litmos from German software giant SAP SE ([SAP](https://www.investopedia.com/markets/quote?tvwidgetsymbol=sap)), announced in August 2022.10 11 Carve-outs tend to fetch lower [valuation multiples](https://www.investopedia.com/terms/m/multiple.asp) than other private equity acquisitions, but can be more complex and riskier.12 13

In a secondary buyout, a private equity firm buys a company from another private equity group rather than a listed company. Such deals have become more common amid increased specialization by private equity firms.14 15 For example, one firm might buy a company to cut costs before selling it to another PE partnership seeking a platform for acquiring complementary businesses.16

Other [exit strategies](https://www.investopedia.com/terms/b/business-exit-strategy.asp) for a private-equity investment include the sale of a portfolio company to one of its competitors as well as its IPO.17

## How to Invest in Private Equity

For those interested in gaining exposure to private equity, several options exist depending on your investor status, available capital, and risk tolerance.

Traditional private equity funds remain primarily the domain of institutional investors and ultra-high-net-worth individuals, commonly requiring multimillion-dollar minimum investments and capital commitments lasting roughly 10 to 12 years. However, more accessible alternatives have emerged for individual investors. Publicly traded private equity firms like Blackstone Inc. ([BX](https://www.investopedia.com/markets/quote?tvwidgetsymbol=BX)), KKR & Co. Inc. ([KKR](https://www.investopedia.com/markets/quote?tvwidgetsymbol=KKR)), Apollo Global Management, Inc. ([APO](https://www.investopedia.com/markets/quote?tvwidgetsymbol=APO)), and Carlyle Group Inc. ([CG](https://www.investopedia.com/markets/quote?tvwidgetsymbol=CG)) offer exposure to the industry through standard brokerage accounts, though their stock performance doesn’t perfectly track their fund returns. Here’s a comparison of investing in private equity funds vs. regular index funds:

Exchange-traded funds ([ETFs](https://www.investopedia.com/terms/e/etf.asp)) focusing on private equity, such as the Invesco Global Listed Private Equity ETF ([PSP](https://www.investopedia.com/markets/quote?tvwidgetsymbol=PSP)), provide exposure to many listed [private equity firms](https://www.investopedia.com/private-equity-etf-risks-11757095) and indirect exposure to the private companies in which they invest.

Before investing, consider that private equity typically involves significant illiquidity, complex fee structures (traditionally “2 and 20“—2% annual management fees plus 20% of profits), and potential tax complications. While the asset class has historically delivered premium returns compared with public markets, performance varies dramatically across firms and strategies, making manager selection critically important when allocating capital to this alternative investment category.

## How Private Equity Is Supposed to Create Value

Private equity firms often develop a plan to increase an investment’s value before acquiring a company. That plan could include dramatic cost cuts or a restructuring, steps the company’s incumbent management may have been reluctant to take. Private equity owners with a limited time to add value before exiting an investment have more of an incentive to make major changes.

The private equity firm may also have special expertise that the company’s prior management lacked. It may help the company adopt new technology or enter additional markets. A private equity firm acquiring a company may bring in its own management team to pursue such initiatives or retain prior managers to execute an agreed-upon plan.

The acquired company can make operational and financial changes without the pressure of having to meet analysts’ [earnings estimates](https://www.investopedia.com/terms/e/earningsestimate.asp) or to please its public shareholders every quarter. Ownership by private equity may allow management to take a longer-term view, unless that conflicts with the new owners’ goal of making the biggest possible [return on investment](https://www.investopedia.com/terms/r/returnoninvestment.asp).

### Tip

A frequent focus of controversy in private equity is the tax treatment of carried interest. Qualifying carried-interest gains may be taxed at lower long-term capital gains rates, generally when the applicable investment is held for more than three years, while management fees and other ordinary compensation are taxed differently. Despite multiple legislative attempts to change this tax treatment, it remains in effect.

### Making Money With Debt

Industry surveys suggest operational improvements have become private equity managers’ main focus and source of added value.18 19

But debt remains an important contributor to private equity returns, even as firms have become less reliant on leverage. Debt used to finance an acquisition reduces the size of the equity commitment and increases the potential return on that investment accordingly, albeit with increased risk.

Private equity managers can also cause the acquired company to take on more debt to accelerate their returns through [a dividend recapitalization](https://www.investopedia.com/terms/d/dividendrecap.asp), which funds a dividend distribution to the private equity owners with borrowed money, a controversial practice.20

## Why Private Equity Draws Criticism

While private equity firms have pushed back against depictions that they strip corporate assets, criticism of the industry has intensified, particularly regarding its impact on health care. For example, a 2025 bipartisan Senate Budget Committee report, led by Senators Sheldon Whitehouse and Chuck Grassley, found that private equity ownership of hospitals had “detrimental effects” on patient care in underserved communities.21 “As our investigation revealed, these financial entities are putting their own profits over patients, leading to health and safety violations, chronic understaffing, and hospital closures,” Whitehouse said.22

The report found that Leonard Green & Partners (LGP), which reported approximately $85 billion in assets under management as of Dec. 31, 2025, received $424 million in distributions and more than $13 million in fees from Prospect Medical Holdings. It linked LGP and Prospect’s broader financial and operational decisions to hospital distress and closures, reduced service availability, and diminished access to essential care in vulnerable communities.23 22

The bipartisan report argues that private equity’s rapid workforce changes following acquisitions often disrupt communities and employees beyond the health care sector. Depending on the transaction type, companies may reduce staff and close or restructure facilities, sometimes prioritizing short-term financial gains over long-term sustainability. Local newspapers reporting on private equity transactions in their communities often fill in details of the costs for more than investors. Private equity ownership of nursing homes in Iowa, for example, has raised concerns about quality of care, though the available evidence does not establish that those facilities were financially stripped. Separately, one academic study estimated that private equity ownership increased short-term mortality among Medicare nursing home patients by 11% relative to non-private-equity ownership.24

In retail, private equity has been blamed for driving dozens of major chains into bankruptcy and eliminating hundreds of thousands of jobs. Separately, a 2019 cross-industry study of 484 public-to-private leveraged buyouts found an approximately 20% bankruptcy rate, compared with 2% among matched control companies.25

Similar damaging effects have been found in other sectors. An industry estimate cited by a 2024 bankruptcy tracker put private equity’s economic contribution at 6.5% of the U.S. economy, though the figure was based on an earlier period rather than a continuously measured 2024 share. In the tracker’s 2024 dataset, private-equity-backed companies accounted for 56% of U.S. corporate bankruptcy filings involving at least $500 million in liabilities and 11% of the qualifying corporate bankruptcies counted. These bankruptcies were tied to about 66,000 layoffs in 2024.26

## How Are Private Equity Funds Managed?

A private equity fund is managed by a general partner (GP). The GP typically controls the fund’s management, although the fund adviser may be legally distinct and investors may retain limited consent or advisory rights. The GP also commonly contributes capital alongside limited partners to give it [skin in the game](https://www.investopedia.com/terms/s/skininthegame.asp), but the amount varies and does not consistently fall between 1% and 3%.

In return, the GP earns a management fee often set at 2% of fund assets, and may be entitled to 20% of fund profits above a preset minimum as incentive compensation, known in [private equity jargon](https://www.investopedia.com/articles/stocks/09/abcs-of-private-equity.asp) as carried interest. [Limited partners](https://www.investopedia.com/terms/l/limited-partner.asp) are investors in the private equity fund, rather than necessarily clients of the firm or adviser, and they generally have [limited liability](https://www.investopedia.com/terms/l/limitedliability.asp).27

## What Is the History of Private Equity Investments?

In 1901, J.P. Morgan bought Carnegie Steel Corp. for $480 million and combined it with Federal Steel Company, National Tube, and several other companies to create U.S. Steel.28

In 1919, Henry Ford used mostly borrowed money to buy out his partners. Minority shareholders John and Horace Dodge had sued after Ford halted special dividends while pursuing expansion plans that included a new auto plant.29 In 1989, KKR bought RJR Nabisco for $25 billion in 1989 in a leveraged buyout.30

## Are Private Equity Firms Regulated?

Private equity funds generally qualify for exclusions from investment-company status under the [Investment Company Act of 1940](https://www.investopedia.com/terms/i/investmentcompanyact.asp) and raise capital through offerings exempt from registration under the [Securities Act of 1933](https://www.investopedia.com/terms/s/securitiesact1933.asp). However, they are not exempt from SEC regulation altogether. Their managers remain subject to applicable provisions of the [Investment Advisers Act of 1940](https://www.investopedia.com/terms/i/investadvact.asp) and the anti-fraud provisions of federal securities laws.31

In February 2022, the SEC proposed new reporting and disclosure requirements for private fund advisers, including private equity fund managers. The SEC adopted final rules in August 2023 that included quarterly statements detailing fund performance, fees, and expenses, as well as annual fund audits. However, the Fifth Circuit vacated those rules on June 5, 2024, and the requirements were not in effect as of Aug. 4, 2026.32 33 34

## The Bottom Line

Private equity stands at a critical juncture in the mid-2020s, with the industry confronting unprecedented challenges despite its continued growth. While private equity assets are projected to more than double from from $512.0 billion in 2025 to $1,237.4 billion by 2034, the sector faces intensifying regulatory scrutiny, investor skepticism because of persistently low distribution rates that reached just 11% of net assets in 2024, and diminishing returns.35

Meanwhile, private equity firms’ use of financial engineering over operational expertise has fueled bipartisan criticism while widening debates over proper oversight of this long-controversial industry.26 4
